solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Pool faucet repositioned in the wrong location (3,2,5)

indicatorNotes.repositioned: Letters that have been repositioned have been moved into new spots, so the fodder is rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A plumber has moved the tap by the swimming pool, and now it sits somewhere silly.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface's own complaint, a tap put in the wrong spot, is the definition, so the clue nearly describes its own answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain idiom: anything not where it belongs is said to be out of place.

entries.clue: Unorthodox way a squash ball may be hit (3-3-4)

annotation.definition2: way a squash ball may be hit

blocks.note: eccentric, bizarre: an informal adjective for it

blocks.clueFragment: way a squash ball may be hit
blocks.note: in squash, players strike the ball so it rebounds from the court's front or side surfaces

annotation.surface: An odd shot on the squash court.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half is literal: squash is played by bouncing the ball off the walls, and that phrase is also slang for weird.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal idiom for eccentric, plus the literal description of a squash rebound: both senses share one phrase.

entries.clue: Couple ultimately don’t show love (3)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately means in the end, so each of the next words gives only its end letter.

blocks.note: the last letters of DON'T and SHOW
love = O, a zero score in tennis

annotation.surface: A pair who, in the end, keep their affection hidden.
annotation.walkthrough: "Don't show love" reads as one phrase about a reserved pair; it splits into two words to be clipped and a zero.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a couple is a pair, a set of that number.

entries.clue: Following a smart diet (7)

blocks.note: f. = following, as in page references (pp. 10 f.)
used as it stands
to smart = to hurt sharply, as a wound does

annotation.surface: Someone is on a clever new eating plan.
annotation.walkthrough: "Smart" looks like an adjective praising the diet; it is the verb, to hurt sharply.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: going without food is the most extreme eating regime.

entries.clue: Start a filling daytime meal (6)

indicatorNotes.filling: A filling sits inside what it fills, so A goes into the meal.

blocks.note: the midday meal, opened after its first letter
used as it stands, placed second

annotation.surface: Tuck into a hearty midday meal to begin.
annotation.walkthrough: "Filling" pretends to describe a substantial lunch; it is the instruction to put A inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to set a project or a ship going is to start it.

entries.clue: Character appearing in Mission: Impossible? (5)

blocks.note: the surface wants a role in the spy film; the setter means a typed symbol
look at the printed title itself: one punctuation mark sits between its two words

annotation.surface: Which role turns up in the spy film Mission: Impossible?
annotation.walkthrough: "Character" suggests a person in the film; it is a typed character, the colon printed in its title.
annotation.definitionFit: Crossword sense: a character is any typed symbol, and the two-dot mark sits in the title between Mission and Impossible.

entries.clue: Acknowledge the audience and prepare for violin performance? (4,1,3)

blocks.note: bend forward from the waist to thank the applause
a violinist picks up the stick strung with horsehair before playing

annotation.surface: A violinist bows to the crowd and then gets ready to play.
annotation.walkthrough: The same three words work twice: the bend at the end of a show, and the stick a violinist picks up.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom for thanking an audience, and a literal reading where the bow is the violinist's stick.

entries.clue: Failures in force leading to cuts (5)

indicatorNotes.leading to: Something leading goes in front, so F comes before the next piece.

blocks.note: F = force, the physics symbol
to lop = to cut off, as with branches

annotation.surface: A police force's failings are blamed on budget cuts.
annotation.walkthrough: "Leading to" is placing, not cause and effect: F leads, standing in front of the word for cuts.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: shows or products that fail badly are called this.

entries.clue: Transfer of data dumps Leonard periodically picked out (6)

indicatorNotes.periodically picked out: Periodically means at regular intervals, so letters are picked out at a steady rhythm.

blocks.note: the 2nd and 4th letters: dUmPs
the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters, keeping the same rhythm across the gap

annotation.surface: Leonard picks items out of rubbish dumps now and then.
annotation.walkthrough: The two words run together as one string, and every second letter from the second onward spells the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Computing term: sending files from a device up to a server is this kind of transfer.

entries.clue: Very poor boys on trek getting lost (5-5)

indicatorNotes.getting lost: Hikers getting lost wander off their set route, so the letters leave their order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Some penniless lads lose their way on a long hike.
annotation.walkthrough: Stony-broke is British slang for having no money at all.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang synonym for penniless.

entries.clue: Cover that’s trimmed at both ends (3)

indicatorNotes.trimmed at both ends: Trimming cuts away the edges, and both ends means the first and last letters go.

blocks.note: the word itself, apostrophe ignored
the opening T and closing S are removed

annotation.surface: A cover with its edges cut back.
annotation.walkthrough: "That's" looks like grammar gluing the clue together; it is the word being trimmed.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by function: headgear covers the head.

entries.clue: Individuals centrally involved in the actual act of stealing (8)

indicatorNotes.centrally: Centrally means at the centre, so only the middle letter of the word is used.
indicatorNotes.involved in: To be involved in something is to be inside it, so that letter goes within the next word.

blocks.note: used as it stands, opened up after its second letter
the middle (6th of 11) letter of INDIVIDUALS, placed after TH
very = actual, as in 'the very man'

annotation.surface: Some people are caught up in the middle of a real robbery.
annotation.walkthrough: "The actual act" reads as one phrase; split it after "the", which holds the I, and "actual" becomes VERY.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the noun for stealing, as larceny or theft.

entries.clue: Working together live on stage? (2,7)

blocks.note: acting jointly, in agreement
a band recorded performing before an audience; the question mark flags the literal reading

annotation.surface: A band performing together in front of an audience.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second sense is a playful literal reading of the idiom.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom for acting jointly, and the literal sense of performing at a gig.

entries.clue: Complaint with joint (6)

blocks.note: w = with, a standard abbreviation
the pivoting joint on a door or lid

annotation.surface: A grumble about an aching joint.
annotation.walkthrough: "Joint" suggests a sore knee; it is the door fitting.
annotation.definitionFit: British and Australian colloquial synonym for a moaning, peevish complaint.

entries.clue: City living initially is good in Paris (6)

indicatorNotes.initially: Initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is taken.
indicatorNotes.in Paris: What is said in Paris is said in French, so the word is translated.

blocks.note: the first letter of LIVING
used as it stands
the French word for good

annotation.surface: Life in the city is good, says a Parisian.
annotation.walkthrough: The Paris in the surface is a decoy city; it only asks for French, and the answer is a different capital, Portugal's.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the capital of Portugal.

entries.clue: Thorough department in one new hospital (2-5)

indicatorNotes.in: One thing in another sits inside it, so the department's letters go within the rest.

blocks.note: the usual abbreviation
one = I, the Roman numeral
n = new, a standard abbreviation
H = hospital, as on road signs; DEPT sits between N and H

annotation.surface: A thorough section of a newly built hospital.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads a hospital department; each word there shrinks to an abbreviation instead: I N (DEPT) H.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a study that goes deep into its subject is thorough.

entries.clue: Tipped to the side, like some significant buildings (6)

blocks.note: what a ship does when it leans over in the water
in Britain, historic buildings are entered on an official register that protects them

annotation.surface: Grand old buildings are leaning over.
annotation.walkthrough: A listed building in Britain is one on the official register of historic buildings, so it cannot be altered freely.
annotation.definitionFit: Nautical verb for leaning, plus the British heritage term for a protected building.

entries.clue: Issue arising from non-union activity? (4,5)

blocks.note: the surface wants a dispute; it means offspring
the surface wants work done without a trade union; the union is a marriage

annotation.surface: A dispute sparked by work done without the trade union.
annotation.walkthrough: The industrial-relations picture is false: "issue" means offspring, and a "union" here is a marriage, not a trade union.
annotation.definitionFit: Euphemism: a child born to unmarried parents, the issue of a non-marital union.

entries.clue: What indicates slight pause in dialogue from sitcom, maybe? (5)

annotation.definition: What indicates slight pause in dialogue

indicatorNotes.from: Taken from means lifted straight out of the words that follow, letters unchanged.

blocks.note: the last three letters of the first word and first two of the second

annotation.surface: What marks a short beat in a comedy script?
annotation.walkthrough: The printed comma in "sitcom, maybe" sits right where the hidden answer spans the break, a neat touch.
annotation.definitionFit: Punctuation by function: this mark tells a reader to take a brief breath.

entries.clue: You and I primarily browse huge source of information online (3)

indicatorNotes.primarily: Primarily means first of all, so only the first letter of the word is taken.

blocks.note: the pronoun for you and I together
the first letter of BROWSE

annotation.surface: Mostly we just surf the internet.
annotation.walkthrough: "Browse" and the definition both belong to the internet, so the surface keeps the wordplay and the answer in one scene.
annotation.definitionFit: Short name for the World Wide Web, the internet's vast store of pages.

entries.clue: Input to AI tool executed without delay (6)

blocks.note: the text a user types into a chatbot
done at once, punctual

annotation.surface: An instruction fed to a chatbot, carried out immediately.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence about a chatbot obeying; it splits into a noun and an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: Modern computing noun for the instruction given to an AI, plus the adjective for punctual.

entries.clue: Alcoholic drink in cup is cold (5)

indicatorNotes.in: What is in a cup is held inside it, so the following letters go inside the vessel.

blocks.note: a po is a chamber pot, a cup-like vessel
used as it stands, inside the vessel
C = cold, as on taps; follows IS inside the vessel

annotation.surface: A drink served in a cup is chilled.
annotation.walkthrough: Pisco is a grape brandy from Peru and Chile. A po is old British slang for a chamber pot.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a South American grape brandy.

entries.clue: Understand where a bishop may have responsibilities (3)

annotation.definition2: where a bishop may have responsibilities

blocks.note: grasp, as in 'I get it'

blocks.clueFragment: where a bishop may have responsibilities
blocks.note: a bishop's diocese, from the Latin for seat

annotation.surface: Grasping what a bishop's job covers.
annotation.walkthrough: A see is the district a bishop governs, named for the bishop's seat.
annotation.definitionFit: Everyday verb for grasping a point, plus the church term for a bishop's district.

entries.clue: Tough cheddar? (4,6)

blocks.note: the retort 'Tough!', meaning bad luck, in its British form
cheddar is a firm, pressed dairy product; the question mark flags an example

annotation.surface: A chewy lump of cheddar.
annotation.walkthrough: "Tough" reads as describing the cheese; it is the retort "Tough!", which the British also say as "Hard cheese!".
annotation.definitionFit: British idiom for tough luck, plus a literal description of cheddar by type.
